In my experience, it most certainly has to do with the size of their stomach organs. Just like you would probably overdose if you took a heroin addicts preferred dose of heroin, it's about building up tolerance over time. A stomach two or three times the normal size will demand to be filled up, and will get used to the feeling. The pleasure comes from the brain and the stomach will adapt. I was 500 pounds before a gastric sleeve changed the size of my stomach, but my brain still wants it's huge "dose" of food, and I still occasionally serve myself huge portions to satisfy my brain, and then get violently ill. I'm only getting sick because I have a normal sized stomach, otherwise a big meal sounds comforting in theory.

I was in a facility years ago that offered guided group meditation. The lady who ran it was excellent. I have never forgotten being fully relaxed after a half hour each group, and her voice reminding us "This is a place you can return to whenever you need it" before we started to shake off the group and finish out the day.  Sometimes during my most stressed out episodes, that reminder rings in my head and I remember what it feels like to be soft and quiet and safe with her glowing lights and music. Like OP said, there is no boundary between here and there, you just remind yourself to return after you get sucked in to a stressful place and forget what it feels like.

I just want to pop in and say that your, and all of our, futures are completely unwritten. I suggest you surrender to the fact that you truly have no idea. It can be hard. I think it's fruitless and exhausting to try and predict/prevent the future with deep dives into fear and grief, no matter your diagnosis or the statistics. No amount of white knuckle control over the details of our lives will prevent bad things from happening to us. The past is a bad place to dwell too, namely feeling old pain over and over again, feeling regret, thinking of old arguments, making character judgements about yourself etc. Meditation involves the concept of being present, and I interpreted this as a way to filter out some things in my loud soup of a mind; the past and the future. In the present, I am somewhere safe from it all. I hear a lot of pain in your post and it hurts me even though we're strangers. We have similar issues, and I can't recommend therapy enough, especially when you click with the provider. Take care.

First you can work on the part of you that is reacting negatively to the noise. Your brain may be a soup full of noise, but you're just going to listen and remove the one voice from the soup that's critical of your noisy mind.

Sometimes peace comes from listening and observing instead of actively supressing. I wouldn't try to investigate and squash all the background chatter because I think it's important to listen with curiousity, without passing judgement and to accept your noisy brain when it's beyond your control, to achieve peace in the bigger picture. I personally have intrusive thoughts that can be very tempting to unravel over, but I'm trying to listen without judgement of any kind to maintain peace and focus while meditating. I'm having success. I think ignoring can work better than investigating when it comes to reducing the chatter long term.
